Why We Moved Our Backups Off the Cloud

By Priya Natarajan — March 14, 2026

For three years we ran nightly snapshots through a managed backup provider and never once tested a restore. It worked, until the week it didn't: a billing dispute silently suspended the account, and forty days of backups vanished along with it. Nobody noticed until we needed them.

That failure forced a rewrite of how we think about durability. A backup you have not restored from is a theory, not a backup. So we rebuilt the whole pipeline around a single rule: every backup job ends with an automated restore into a scratch directory, and the job fails loudly if the restored file does not pass a checksum and a row-count sanity check against the live database.

The mechanics are almost boring. A nightly cron job runs VACUUM INTO against a temporary file, compresses it, copies it to two independent object stores in different regions, and then immediately pulls one of those copies back down and opens it read-only to confirm it is a valid SQLite file with the expected table counts. If any step fails, an alert fires before the sun comes up, not three months later during an actual outage.

We also stopped trusting a single provider's definition of "durable." Object storage guarantees are about the bytes you already wrote, not about your account still existing tomorrow. Two independent providers, two independent billing relationships, and a third copy on a physical disk in a drawer turned out to be cheaper than the peace of mind it bought.

None of this is exotic. It is the same lesson every operations team learns eventually: untested backups are a false sense of security, and the fix is not a better vendor, it is a restore drill that runs automatically and fails the pipeline the moment it stops proving anything.
